Update and proposal

One declaration first. As you know, I was a CGL service user. CGL funded my residential rehab place, and its Cambridgeshire service is part of my own recovery history. 01

We met in April. You told me to send everything over.

Why it took me until now.

I didn’t do that. Not because of any issue, simply because I wasn’t ready, as we established together at the time. I took the advice, spent the time getting set up properly and putting my idea through some rigorous checks. Now I’m ready, with a serious plan and proposal for your consideration.

As we both know and understand, there is rarely a single root cause of addiction. It grows out of a mix of trauma, mental health, genes and environment, and it is now widely seen as a complex condition of the brain, not a lack of willpower. But, as I mentioned in our meeting, there is something I experienced that I believe is being missed and I have a documented history and an actual letter stating it.

In April 2026 an independent consultant psychiatrist wrote to the CPFT Adult ADHD Team about my care and named the pattern in one sentence:

“Adult ADHD previously complicated with excess alcohol use to self-medicate inadequately managed ADHD symptoms.”

Read the order of it. Not ADHD plus alcohol, treated separately. ADHD — complicated by self-medication. That letter is about me. It proves that what happened to me has a name, in writing.

I had a life-changing moment, but one man’s experience is not evidence about a population, and I am not going to pretend it is. That is why I think the question is worth asking. It is not why I think I already know the answer.

I believe for a significant, high-cost, identifiable group of adults — and for me, until mine was treated — untreated ADHD is driving relapse by recycling and fanning the fire of the addiction, regardless of origin. The chaos, crises and costs are just what arrives in view. The others are still trapped — and this is my plan to help them.

My simple but challenging idea starts with the people already in the problem. I use the correction to my own journey: an intervention that gets the driver found and treated far earlier — before the addiction work begins. Continuity, my infrastructure, is the non-clinical layer that holds a person through assessment, diagnosis and medication, if prescribed, and through the days between the services already treating them — and it carries the whole thing: from the intervention through to a pre-medicated brain that receives increased connection, education and continuous behavioural reinforcement. One that can finally hold recovery and find its own way Out The Other Side. The way I did, without what it cost me to get there. In time, the same approach could keep people away from the addiction door altogether — but that is where it leads, not where it starts.

This is a plan to stop what happened to me happening to the next person, and cut the huge associated costs crippling the whole system, not just the NHS.

I survived, but I know there are people in the services you commission right now who cannot do what I did. They don’t have the resources, the language, the luck or the fight left in them. I am determined to go back and help them. It’s like my whole life has been market research for OTOS.

Below is the final documentation I was going to send — and still will, when we get to that stage.

Part of that was designing a pre-pilot that would stand up to scrutiny — a bounded demonstration, designed to test what the report finds and produce evidence for a pilot. It’s budgeted low on purpose, so I would never be asking you to fund a full pilot on a hunch and my experience alone. Then I remembered what you said about small pots of money possibly being available, just as the media attention and NHS announcements around ADHD were growing, with still very little said about the link to addiction. So I added an even lower entry: the first step, small and self-contained — a fixed-price report, £4,950. It is an easier yes for you, ahead of any investment in my solution, and it will establish the facts, whatever it finds. Something useful to both of us: the report is the Council’s to own and use, in a field where, as NHS England’s own Taskforce says, no published papers yet exist on the contemporary costs of untreated ADHD in the UK. And if the question holds up, a chance for Cambridgeshire, and the wider Central East area, to be UK leaders on this rather than follow, with you as the one who set it going.

02

What I have been doing since April

A company, a board, the facts checked, and the services starting to see it.

  1. I set up OTOS Digital Ltd, so you would be dealing with a registered company, not with an individual. I have also built an Advisory Board, including my father, a best friend in the education space (who witnessed everything, including the significant changes this year) and another friend, a highly experienced banking security developer.   3. Some services have finally seen it. CGL and CRS have their own pages, sent on 21 and 22 September. The ADHD Team, Alcohol Liaison at Addenbrooke’s, RCE Wellbeing Hub and Mind / WorkWell are all getting their invitations: to contribute their thoughts first. These target partners will all receive their versions over the next week or so. I am asking for their support of the three-stage plan, and requesting meetings with everyone.
  4. The research route is open, on both fronts: business and personal. I was invited into the APPIE network, the NIHR addictions research unit’s lived-experience network, and I am now a registered member, available to contribute to addiction research projects.
  5. I recently wrote to Professor Samuele Cortese at the University of Southampton — in 2022 he was ranked number one worldwide for expertise on ADHD — asking whether the question stands up scientifically, including whether it doesn’t, and whether he would consider acting as academic lead or principal investigator. That route is secondary, but complementary, and both could make real change. Funded research wrapped around my technology gets the question properly named, and proven or disproven — but realistically it’s a two-year project. The problem needs faster action, and that leaves the first-mover opportunity with Cambridgeshire Public Health — to make a real impact much sooner.

While looking for anything comparable, I found a recent French study with a striking result.

61.3%*

of people already in addiction treatment showed improvement in their addictive disorders six months after the ADHD underneath was diagnosed.

That success wasn’t only down to medication. The figure includes people who improved simply by being formally assessed for ADHD — found, targeted and held in a dedicated way while they waited, carrying on with their addiction work. The response after ADHD diagnosis was excellent. That percentage is hard to ignore, and once you have seen it you cannot unsee it. Imagine if we could achieve results like this in Cambridgeshire. The national potential is exciting. The right place to start is here, with the facts.

What the national guidance says
  • NICE NG87, recommendation 1.2.1 names people with a history of substance misuse, and adults with a mental health condition, among the groups who may have increased ADHD prevalence. Recommendation 1.4.3 uses the words substance misuse and self-medication.
  • RCPsych CR235, s11.1 records that substance misuse “may be twice as common among individuals with ADHD as in the general population and tends to begin earlier”, and that individuals with untreated ADHD “may also describe self-medicating with illicit substances”.
  • The Royal College of Psychiatrists says significant comorbid substance misuse should be managed jointly between adult and addiction services (CR235).
  • Neither body says how often the overlap is being missed locally. That is the question this asks.

The medication does not do the recovery work. It creates the conditions where it can finally land — and published CGL material suggests prior development of an ADHD assessment pathway within a substance-use / criminal-justice context is underway (Hammond, Murphy & Huke, Clinical Psychology Forum, November 2024; practice development, not a trial). So, it’s starting. OTOS is not proposing diagnostic duplication; it is proposing continuity visibility between services so agreed next steps are less likely to disappear between silos.

I know what the guidance says. Stabilise the substance misuse first; in uncontrolled and chaotic use, stimulants are not routinely recommended (CR235). The same guidance says that “when prescribed stimulants are used appropriately, there is little evidence of patients becoming dependent, and indeed treating ADHD may reduce the lifetime risk of developing a substance use disorder” (CR235 §11.1). I was stabilised first, more than once, and each time the driver went untreated. The sequence belongs to the clinicians. What is required is cohort identification, upstream intervention, and increased connection and continuity.

04

The Continuity Infrastructure

A non-clinical layer that holds the thread between services.

Every service owns its own episode. Nobody owns the time between them. That is not a criticism of anyone — it is how the system is built. But it means the most dangerous period in this journey is the one period that belongs to nobody. It is not a gap in care. It is unowned risk.

OTOS asks no organisation to take on that risk, that liability or that caseload. It fills the space intelligently with continuous connection, pre-agreed service updates, and behavioural reinforcement with addiction education — so the gap stops belonging to nobody and becomes genuinely useful. The person is no longer stuck on their own. Not joining up the services — holding the person across them, and updating them with agreed, Continuity-only updates.

The clinical notes stay where they are. The continuity signal travels. Every drift signal requires a human review decision before any action. No autonomous clinical output.

It is consent-led: nobody is on it without agreeing to be. The person opts in, agrees the services can share access to their thread, and the thread only ever shows specific, pre-agreed information.

What the OTOS Continuity layer is, and what it is not

✕ What OTOS is not

  • A clinical service, diagnosis tool or treatment
  • An EPR or NHS record — no record access, no write-back
  • A replacement for any existing service
  • A finished product asking for endorsement
  • A guaranteed cash-release claim — savings are modelled potential

✓ What OTOS is

  • A non-clinical continuity layer around services that already exist
  • A small, bounded demonstrator — built to prove pilot readiness
  • A way to test whether redirected spend reduces repeat demand
  • Built from lived experience of this exact pathway

For the services, in practice: waiting-list silence becomes a signal instead of a blind spot, micro check-ins keep contact going between keyworker calls, and a person reviews every signal before anything is done.

  • OTOS Continuity™ is non-clinical continuity infrastructure.
  • OTOS does not diagnose; does not prescribe or manage medication; does not treat addiction or deliver therapy; does not make clinical decisions; does not automate safeguarding decisions.
  • OTOS does not replace existing services; does not create a shared clinical record; does not merge partner records; does not give partners access to each other’s systems.
  • Partner teams retain decisions, duties and responsibilities. Existing service relationships remain separate.
  • OTOS does not build, own or operate a pathway.
05

The cost that is already being paid

The cost does not disappear. It moves to a worse budget line.

The national anchor is not mine and does not need to be. The independent ADHD Taskforce, reporting to NHS England, already wrote it for me and put the economic cost to individuals and government at "at least £17 billion" a year and named the drivers: unemployment, crime, substance misuse.

In the same report the Taskforce says this: “No published papers on the contemporary costs of untreated ADHD in the UK exist yet.”

Where that money goes is not new to you

And that is the preventable second battle. People wait with unmanaged ADHD. Then they reappear — in A&E, in addiction services, in mental-health crisis, in collapse, in detox, in rehab, in housing pressure, in benefits queues, in police contact, probation and courts, often ending up in jail. By the time the system catches up, the original need has become much more expensive, and much harder to unwind. None of that is a projection. It is this year's spend, on people your services already know by name, and it recurs because the driver underneath was never treated.

If CGL had just known I was in and out of A&E and waiting on the ADHD medication-review list — with an agreement to speed up my ADHD treatment, instead of the backlog trapping me in addiction and costing every other service too — I could have avoided so much pain and loss, and the system wouldn’t have spent nearly as much.

Nothing in that sentence asks for a new service to be funded — it is about the costs. Two services were already treating me, while I am still, to this day, waiting on another. No one could — or can — see the whole picture, or the whole journey.

And I’m still inside the problem. Diagnosed in 2020, referred in 2021, once on shared care — and to this day the letters A-D-H-D do not appear anywhere on MyChart, in my NHS Login, or even on my GP record. Incredibly, the system still cannot see the driver in me. As I explained, I have tried other surgeries and been challenged with the non-RTC route issue, so my parents still pick up the bill for my private ADHD medication — another ripple cost, to the people around me.

The only number of my own is my estimate for alcohol, and it is labelled as mine. Every local figure below is built from a published denominator and a labelled assumption, and it is shown with its working so you can disagree with any single step.

—

Run it yourself

How well would it have to work to be worth finding out?

When I first put this together, I couldn’t believe the enormity of the numbers, so I built you a calculator to run yourself rather than picking my own. One number, and it is yours to set. Not my model — one published local count, two published per-person costs, one estimate of my own for alcohol, and a figure you choose.

The pool is the 4,690 adults already in structured addiction treatment across Cambridgeshire and Peterborough. It is not the cohort, and it only counts those officially in treatment — there are many more outside it, creating the same costs, possibly more. You choose the share: if unrecognised ADHD — diagnosed or not — is driving the cycle for this share of them…

If 10% · approx 469 adults

Costs

ADHD — £17,000 a year each 469 × £17,000 = £7,973,000

Alcohol — the 2,120 in treatment for alcohol 212 × £25,000 = £5,300,000

Heroin and crack — the 1,960 in opiate treatment 196 × £27,000 = £5,292,000

Then the potential saving, every year, could be up to £18,565,000

That is a potential saving, not a promise. It is the public spending already attached to a group that size — today, across budget lines that never speak to each other. How much of it could move is the question. If a number is going to persuade you, it should be one you set yourself.

And that is before the ripple — and the ripple is human before it is financial.

You know the savings land across several budget lines at once — which is probably part of why no single budget holder has ever had a big enough reason to fund the fix.

Medicating this cohort properly may not just save the system money. It could be a double win: the system ends up up, not down, and not break-even.
Where every number comes from

Nothing on this page is an OTOS result. Everything is either a published figure with its source named, my own estimate for alcohol, labelled as mine, or a number you set yourself. Here is each one.

4,690 — the pool: every adult in structured addiction treatment, not the cohort

NDTMS 2024/25. Cambridgeshire 2,980 plus Peterborough 1,710. A published count, not an estimate.

1,960 — the adults in opiate treatment, part of the 4,690

NDTMS 2024/25, Cambridgeshire and Peterborough combined. A published count, not an estimate.

£17,000 — additional public cost per adult with ADHD, per year

Report of the independent ADHD Taskforce, NHS England, Part 1, 20 June 2025. Danish patient registry data, compared against same-sex siblings. Three things it is not: it is not UK data; it is a sibling comparison rather than a whole-system cost; and it describes adults with ADHD, not adults with ADHD and addiction. That last one cuts in my favour and I still will not assert it — the cohort I am describing would plausibly cost more, not less, and that is an argument to test, not a number to print.

£27,000 — public cost per heroin or crack user, per year

Review of Drugs evidence pack, Public Health England and Home Office, for the Dame Carol Black review, February 2020, p.14, 2017–18 prices. Police and health care only; the same slide gives £58,000 once lost productivity and quality of life are added. The slide cites unpublished PHE analysis. Applied only to the 1,960 in opiate treatment.

£25,000 — alcohol, per person in crisis, per year: my own estimate, not published

I could not find a published cost per dependent drinker per year. The national figure, £27.44 billion a year for England (Institute of Alcohol Studies, May 2024), is the harm caused by everyone who drinks, so it cannot honestly be split per person.

So I have used my own experience again. My estimate is approximately £25,000 a year in crisis — housing, council tax, ambulances, police attendances, A&E, court costs and detoxes — and I have used that figure to represent my specific segment of the cohort.

Applied to the 2,120 in treatment for alcohol: 1,405 for alcohol only and 715 for alcohol with non-opiate drugs (NDTMS 2024/25).

The figures overlap in part — all three count some crime and health costs — so the total is a ceiling. That is why it says up to.

The slider — and why there is only one

The slider is your own estimate of the share of the pool with ADHD, diagnosed or not, applied the same way to every group. There is no verified prevalence figure for ADHD within UK addiction-treatment populations. None. So, apart from my alcohol estimate, the model uses only published figures, and lets you supply the other uncertain term: the share, which is the very thing the report sets out to find out. The result is arithmetic, not a forecast, not a projection, and not a claim about what Cambridgeshire would save.

06

The local ask · Cambridgeshire County Council

What I am asking you to commission first.

You said you do test things at a small size, and you gave me the example yourself: the CGL street team, out helping people who just can’t get there and will never make it through the door of a building. That’s excellent, innovative — and it’s the argument.

A service realised its cohort was not reaching it, so it went to them. That is the same problem one step earlier: the thread breaks between services, so someone has to hold it. You already fund that logic. The report asks what is underneath the cohort it is aimed at — and the others like me, who are sat there right now.

A commissioned research report. It asks one question:

Is ADHD materially under-recognised among people at the intersection of addiction and mental-health complexity in Cambridgeshire — and what would the system need to know before deciding whether to act?

That question sets up the next one, which is mine: what intervening earlier does to repeat relapse and system-wide costs. That is for the pre-pilot to answer, if the report says it is worth asking.

And the report has to be able to conclude that there is no signal.

If the honest answer is that this cohort has already been characterised, or that the overlap isn’t there locally, that is what it will say — and you will have paid £4,950 to close a question rather than open one. A piece of research that can only reach one conclusion isn’t research, and it isn’t worth your money.
